column9: A math book sits at rest on Storm's desk. According to Newton's 1st law, what will the book do if the forces on it stay balanced?
column14: Slowly start to slide off the desk
column16: Speed up a little over time
column17: Start moving at a constant speed
column28: An object at rest stays at rest unless acted upon by an unbalanced force. Balanced forces (Fg down, FN up) cause no change in motion, so the book stays put.
column29: What does the 1st law say about an object that starts at rest?

column9: The resistance of an object to a change in its motion is called ___.
column28: Inertia is the resistance of an object to change motion. The more mass an object has, the more inertia it has.
column29: Newton's 1st law is sometimes called the law of this.

column9: Which change would give a wagon more inertia?
column14: Pulling it at a faster speed
column17: Loading more mass into it
column28: More mass = more inertia. Speed and color do not change inertia, and taking it to the Moon changes its weight, not its mass.
column29: Inertia depends on only one property of an object. Which one?

column9: An object at rest has no forces acting on it.
column28: False. A book at rest on a table has gravity (Fg) pulling down and the normal force (FN) pushing up. The forces are balanced, so the book's motion does not change.
column29: Think of a book on a table. Is gravity still pulling on it?

column9: Which law says that the acceleration of an object depends on the net force acting on it and the object's mass?
column14: Newton's 1st law
column17: Law of conservation of momentum
column28: Newton's 2nd law: the acceleration of an object depends on the net force acting on it and the object's mass (F = ma). The 1st law is about inertia and the 3rd law is about action-reaction pairs.
column29: Which law has an equation with force, mass, and acceleration?

column9: In the tablecloth trick, a magician yanks the cloth out quickly and the dishes stay on the table. Why do the dishes stay in place?
column14: The dishes' inertia keeps them at rest
column15: The tablecloth pushes the dishes down
column16: Pulling fast makes gravity on the dishes stronger
column17: The dishes have no mass while the cloth moves
column28: The dishes are at rest and their inertia resists a change in motion. The cloth slides out so fast that friction acts for only a tiny moment, too short to get the dishes moving much.
column29: Were the dishes moving or at rest before the trick? What does the 1st law say they want to keep doing?

column9: A bowling ball is harder to start moving AND harder to stop than a tennis ball.
column28: True. More mass = more inertia, and inertia resists any change in motion, both starting and stopping. The bowling ball has much more mass than the tennis ball.
column29: Which ball has more mass, and what does mass tell you about inertia?

column9: If the forces on a rolling shopping cart are balanced, the cart keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction.
column28: True. Balanced forces mean no change in motion. An object in motion stays in motion at a constant speed in a straight line unless acted upon by an unbalanced force.
column29: Balanced forces cause no change in motion. Is the cart already moving?

column9: When the forces on an object are balanced, the net force on the object is ___ N.
column28: Balanced forces cancel out (like a tug-of-war with equal pulls), so the net force is 0 N and the motion does not change.
column29: Equal forces in opposite directions: subtract them. What is left?

column9: Why does a seatbelt protect you when a car stops suddenly?
column14: The seatbelt pushes the car so it stops faster
column15: The car's brakes push your body backward
column16: Your body keeps moving forward because of inertia until the belt stops you
column17: Your weight increases when the car stops
column28: Your body is in motion and stays in motion (inertia) when the car stops. The seatbelt supplies the unbalanced force that stops you instead of the dashboard or windshield.
column29: The car stops. What does your body want to keep doing?

column9: Match each quantity to its unit.
column14: Force :: newtons (N)
column17: Velocity :: meters per second (m/s)
column28: Force is in newtons (N), mass in kilograms (kg), acceleration in m/s^{2}, and velocity in m/s. Acceleration has seconds squared because it is a change in velocity (m/s) per second.
column29: Acceleration is how much the velocity (m/s) changes every second.

column9: Maya pushes a cart with a certain net force. If she doubles the force and the mass stays the same, what happens to the cart's acceleration?
column14: It is cut in half
column17: It becomes four times as large
column28: Force and acceleration have a direct relationship: if you double the force, you double the acceleration (a = F/m).
column29: Look at a = F ÷ m. If the top number doubles, what happens to the answer?

column9: Inertia is a force that keeps objects moving.
column28: False. Inertia is not a force; it is a property of matter (resistance to change in motion) that depends on mass. A moving object needs no force to keep moving at a constant speed in a straight line.
column29: Is inertia measured in newtons, or does it depend on mass?

column9: A hockey puck slides a long way across smooth ice after it is hit. Which best explains this?
column14: The force from the stick stays inside the puck as it slides
column15: The puck has no inertia while it is on ice
column16: Gravity pulls the puck forward across the ice
column17: Ice has very little friction, so almost no unbalanced force slows the puck
column28: An object in motion stays in motion unless an unbalanced force acts on it. Smooth ice gives very little friction, so the puck keeps going. The stick's force ends the moment the puck leaves the stick.
column29: What force usually slows a sliding object down, and how much of it is there on ice?

column9: Students are standing on a moving bus when the driver slams on the brakes. Which way do the students lurch?
column14: Forward
column17: They do not move at all
column28: The students were moving forward with the bus. When the bus stops, their inertia keeps them moving forward.
column29: Before the brakes, which way were the students moving?

column9: Storm pushes a 45 kg four-wheeler so that it accelerates at 1.8 m/s^{2}. What net force acts on the four-wheeler? Answer in N.
column28: Formula: F = m × a. Set up: F = 45 kg × 1.8 m/s^{2}. Answer: 81 N.
column29: Force = mass × acceleration.

column9: Mrs. Thorpe's 1,350 kg car accelerates at 3.2 m/s^{2} as she merges onto Hwy 29. What net force acts on the car? Answer in N.
column28: Formula: F = m × a. Set up: F = 1,350 kg × 3.2 m/s^{2}. Answer: 4320 N.
column29: Multiply the mass in kg by the acceleration.

column9: An electric scooter and its rider are pushed by a net force of 540 N and accelerate at 3.6 m/s^{2}. What is their total mass? Answer in kg.
column28: Formula: m = F ÷ a. Set up: m = 540 N ÷ 3.6 m/s^{2}. Answer: 150 kg. Multiplying (1,944) is the common mistake.
column29: Cover m in the force triangle: Mass = Force ÷ Acceleration.

column9: Addy pushes a loaded shopping cart at Walmart with a net force of 84 N, and it accelerates at 2.4 m/s^{2}. What is the mass of the cart? Answer in kg.
column28: Formula: m = F ÷ a. Set up: m = 84 N ÷ 2.4 m/s^{2}. Answer: 35 kg.
column29: Mass = Force ÷ Acceleration.

column9: A semi truck has a mass of 38,500 kg. Its engine provides a net force of 52,000 N. What is its acceleration? Answer in m/s^{2}.
column28: Formula: a = F ÷ m. Set up: a = 52,000 N ÷ 38,500 kg. Answer: 1.35 m/s^{2}.
column29: Acceleration = Force ÷ Mass. Put the force on top.

column9: Jacob and his bike have a total mass of 72 kg. He pedals with a net force of 180 N. What is his acceleration? Answer in m/s^{2}.
column28: Formula: a = F ÷ m. Set up: a = 180 N ÷ 72 kg. Answer: 2.5 m/s^{2}.
column29: Acceleration = Force ÷ Mass.

column9: A 6.0 kg bowling ball is pushed with a net force of 15 N. What is its acceleration?
column28: Formula: a = F ÷ m. Set up: a = 15 N ÷ 6.0 kg. Answer: 2.5 m/s^{2}. 2.5 m/s has the right number but is a velocity unit; 90 multiplies and 0.40 divides backwards.
column29: Use a = F ÷ m, then check the unit: acceleration is not measured in m/s.

column9: Saffron pulls a wagon with a steady net force, and it accelerates at 3.0 m/s^{2}. Her little brother climbs in, which doubles the total mass. She pulls with the same force. What is the new acceleration?
column28: Mass and acceleration have an inverse relationship: if you double the mass, you cut the acceleration in half. 3.0 ÷ 2 = 1.5 m/s^{2}.
column29: With the same force, does more mass make the wagon speed up more or less?

column9: A sled accelerates at 1.4 m/s^{2} when Wyatt pulls it. If the net force is tripled and the mass stays the same, what is the new acceleration? Answer in m/s^{2}.
column28: Force and acceleration are directly related: triple the force → triple the acceleration. 1.4 m/s^{2} × 3 = 4.2 m/s^{2}.
column29: Direct relationship: whatever you do to the force, you do to the acceleration.

column9: Match each situation to the Newton's law that best explains it.
column14: A book stays at rest on a shelf until someone pushes it :: Newton's 1st law
column15: A full shopping cart needs a bigger push than an empty one to speed up the same amount :: Newton's 2nd law
column16: A rocket pushes gas down and the gas pushes the rocket up :: Newton's 3rd law
column28: 1st law = an object stays at rest or in motion (inertia). 2nd law = acceleration depends on force and mass (F = ma). 3rd law = equal and opposite action-reaction forces on two objects.
column29: Is the situation about inertia, about force and mass changing acceleration, or about two objects pushing on each other?

column9: A car is hit from behind and jumps forward. Without a headrest, the driver's head would snap backward. Which law explains why the head snaps back?
column14: Newton's 3rd law
column17: Law of conservation of mass
column28: The head is at rest and its inertia keeps it at rest while the car and seat move forward, so it seems to snap back. That is Newton's 1st law; the headrest pushes the head forward with the car.
column29: Was the head moving before the hit? What does inertia say it wants to keep doing?

column9: Jae kicks a soccer ball gently, then kicks it again much harder. The harder kick makes the ball speed up much more. Which law best explains this?
column14: Newton's 1st law
column17: Law of inertia
column28: A bigger force on the same mass gives a bigger acceleration (F = ma). That is Newton's 2nd law. The 1st law (law of inertia) is about motion staying the same, and the 3rd law is about action-reaction pairs.
column29: The ball's mass stayed the same. What changed, and which law connects force to acceleration?

column9: Which of these are examples of inertia (Newton's 1st law)? Select all that apply.
column14: Ketchup comes out when you swing the bottle down and stop it suddenly
column15: A coin on a card drops into a cup when the card is flicked away quickly
column16: A runner keeps going for several steps after crossing the finish line
column17: A swimmer pushes back on the wall and the wall pushes her forward
column18: A heavy bowling ball speeds up less than a light one with the same push
column19: A balloon shoots forward as air rushes out the back
column28: Ketchup, coin, and runner all keep doing what they were doing (moving or at rest) because of inertia. The swimmer and balloon are action-reaction pairs (3rd law), and the bowling ball comparison is F = ma (2nd law).
column29: For each one ask: is something just continuing its motion (or rest), or are forces and masses being compared?

column9: A space probe drifting far from any planet, with no forces acting on it, will gradually slow down and stop.
column28: False. An object in motion stays in motion at a constant speed in a straight line unless acted upon by an unbalanced force. With no friction or air resistance, nothing slows the probe.
column29: On Earth, what slows moving things down? Is that force in deep space?

column9: In a tug-of-war, Team A pulls the rope left with 450 N and Team B pulls right with 450 N. The rope started at rest. What happens to the rope?
column14: It accelerates toward Team B
column16: It moves with a net force of 900 N
column17: It stays at rest because the forces are balanced
column28: Opposite directions subtract: 450 N − 450 N = 0 N. Balanced forces cause no change in motion, so the rope stays at rest. Adding to get 900 N is the common mistake.
column29: Forces in opposite directions: add or subtract?

column9: Put the steps for finding an object's mass from its force and acceleration in order.
column14: Plug in the force and the acceleration
column15: Write the answer with units of kg
column16: Write the formula F = m × a
column17: Divide the force by the acceleration
column28: Formula (F = m × a, so m = F ÷ a) → set up with the force and acceleration → divide → answer with units (kg).
column29: Use the Formula / Set up / Answer format. What do you do last?

column9: Which of these could be a correct answer for a force?
column17: 25 kg·m/s
column28: 1 N = 1 kg·m/s^{2} (mass × acceleration). kg is mass, m/s^{2} is acceleration, and kg·m/s is momentum.
column29: Force = mass × acceleration. Multiply the units of mass and acceleration.

column9: Wyatt drops a 2.5 kg pumpkin off the bleachers. Ignoring air resistance, it falls with an acceleration of 9.8 m/s^{2}. Using F = ma, what is the force of gravity on the pumpkin? Answer in N.
column28: Formula: F = m × a. Set up: F = 2.5 kg × 9.8 m/s^{2}. Answer: 24.5 N. Dividing (0.26) is the common mistake.
column29: The acceleration of a falling object is g. Force = mass × acceleration.

column9: If the net force stays the same, mass and acceleration have an ___ relationship.
column28: Inverse: when mass goes up, acceleration goes down (double the mass → half the acceleration). Force and acceleration are the ones with a direct relationship.
column29: Same push on an empty cart and a full cart: when mass goes up, what happens to acceleration?

column9: A 1,200 kg car slows down at a rate of 4.5 m/s^{2} when the driver brakes. What is the size of the net force on the car? Answer in N.
column28: Formula: F = m × a. Set up: F = 1,200 kg × 4.5 m/s^{2}. Answer: 5400 N (pointing backward, opposite the motion).
column29: Slowing down is still an acceleration. Force = mass × acceleration.

column9: Wyatt kicks a 0.43 kg soccer ball that starts at rest. His foot is in contact with the ball for 0.012 s, and the ball leaves at 24 m/s. What force did he apply? Answer in N.
column29: Find acceleration first (a = change in velocity ÷ time), then use it to calculate force.

column9: A 1,500 kg pickup speeds up from 0 m/s to 27 m/s in 9.0 s on Hwy 29. What net force acts on it? Answer in N.
column29: Step 1: a = Δv ÷ t. Step 2: F = m × a.

column9: A 0.17 kg hockey puck at rest is hit by a stick. The stick touches the puck for 0.025 s, and the puck leaves at 32 m/s. What force did the stick apply? Answer in N.
column29: You need the acceleration before you can use F = ma.

column9: A 62 kg skier slows from 15 m/s to a stop in 5.0 s. What is the size of the net force that stopped her? Answer in N.
column28: Step 1: a = Δv ÷ t = (15 − 0) m/s ÷ 5.0 s = 3 m/s^{2} (slowing down). Step 2: F = m × a = 62 kg × 3 m/s^{2} = 186 N.
column29: Find how fast her velocity changes each second, then multiply by her mass.

column9: A 2,000 kg truck starts from rest. A net force of 5,000 N acts on it for 8.0 s. How fast is it going at the end? Answer in m/s.
column28: Step 1: a = F ÷ m = 5,000 N ÷ 2,000 kg = 2.5 m/s^{2}. Step 2: Δv = a × t = 2.5 m/s^{2} × 8.0 s = 20 m/s, so it ends at 20 m/s.
column29: Work backward: F = ma gives the acceleration, and acceleration tells how much the speed changes each second.

column9: A lab cart goes from rest to 6.0 m/s in 1.5 s. The net force on it is 36 N. What is the cart's mass? Answer in kg.
column29: Find the acceleration from the speeds and time first, then use Mass = Force ÷ Acceleration.

column9: Jae pushes a 25 kg box to the right with 140 N. Friction pushes on the box 65 N to the left. What is the box's acceleration? Answer in m/s^{2}.
column28: Net force: 140 N − 65 N = 75 N right. Formula: a = F ÷ m. Set up: a = 75 N ÷ 25 kg. Answer: 3 m/s^{2} to the right. Using 140 N instead of the net force is the common mistake.
column29: Find the net force first (opposite directions subtract), then use a = F ÷ m.

column9: Addy wants a 40 kg crate to accelerate to the right at 1.5 m/s^{2}. Friction on the crate is 70 N to the left. How hard must she push to the right? Answer in N.
column28: Step 1: net force needed: F = m × a = 40 kg × 1.5 m/s^{2} = 60 N. Step 2: her push must beat friction AND supply that net force: 60 N + 70 N = 130 N.
column29: F = ma gives the net force. Her push minus friction has to equal that net force.

column9: On the Moon, objects fall with an acceleration of 1.6 m/s^{2}. An astronaut's weight on the Moon is 136 N. What is the astronaut's mass? Answer in kg.
column28: Formula: m = F ÷ a. Set up: m = 136 N ÷ 1.6 m/s^{2}. Answer: 85 kg. Her mass is the same on Earth; only her weight changes.
column29: Weight is the force, and the Moon's g is the acceleration. Mass = Force ÷ Acceleration.

column9: A 4.0 kg cart accelerates at 6.0 m/s^{2} when pushed. The exact same net force is used on a 12 kg cart. What is the 12 kg cart's acceleration? Answer in m/s^{2}.
column28: Step 1: F = m × a = 4.0 kg × 6.0 m/s^{2} = 24 N. Step 2: a = F ÷ m = 24 N ÷ 12 kg = 2 m/s^{2}. Shortcut: 3 times the mass → one-third the acceleration.
column29: Find the force from the first cart, then use it on the second cart.

column9: Storm doubles the net force on a cart AND doubles the cart's mass at the same time. What happens to the acceleration?
column14: It doubles
column17: It becomes four times as large
column28: Doubling the force doubles the acceleration, and doubling the mass cuts it in half. The two changes cancel: a = 2F ÷ 2m = F ÷ m, so the acceleration stays the same.
column29: Do each change one at a time. What does each one do to the acceleration?

column9: Two carts are pushed with the same net force. Cart A accelerates 3 times as much as Cart B. How do their masses compare?
column14: Cart A has 3 times the mass of Cart B
column15: Cart B has 3 times the mass of Cart A
column17: Cart B has one-third the mass of Cart A
column28: With the same force, mass and acceleration are inverse. The cart that accelerates less has more mass, so Cart B has 3 times the mass of Cart A.
column29: Same push: does the heavier cart accelerate more or less?

column9: Addy calculates the force on an 8.0 kg box accelerating at 2.5 m/s^{2}. She gets 3.2 N. What mistake did she make?
column14: She used m/s instead of m/s^{2}
column16: She forgot to multiply by 9.8 m/s^{2}
column17: She divided the mass by the acceleration instead of multiplying
column28: 8.0 ÷ 2.5 = 3.2, so she divided. Formula: F = m × a. Set up: F = 8.0 kg × 2.5 m/s^{2}. Answer: 20 N.
column29: Try 8.0 and 2.5 with each operation. Which one gives her answer?

column9: Which objects have an unbalanced force acting on them? Select all that apply.
column14: A car speeding up on an on-ramp
column15: A car cruising at a steady 25 m/s on a straight road
column16: A skydiver falling at a constant velocity
column17: A bus turning a corner at a steady speed
column18: A book at rest on a shelf
column19: A soccer ball slowing down as it rolls across the grass
column28: An unbalanced force changes motion: speeding up, slowing down, or changing direction. The car speeding up, the bus turning (direction changes), and the slowing ball all change motion. Constant velocity in a straight line and at rest mean balanced forces.
column29: Look for any change in speed OR direction. A steady speed in a straight line, or at rest, means balanced.

column9: A dresser is being slid to the right across carpet. Its FBD shows Fapp 60 N right, Ff 60 N left, and FN up and Fg down with equal-length arrows. Which describes its motion?
column14: Speeding up to the right
column16: Moving right at a constant velocity
column17: Speeding up to the left
column28: Horizontal: 60 N − 60 N = 0 N; vertical: FN and Fg cancel. Net force is zero, so its motion does not change: it keeps sliding right at a constant velocity (1st law). It does not need a bigger forward arrow to keep moving.
column29: Find the net force left-right and up-down. What does zero net force mean for an object that is already moving?

column9: Wyatt shakes his wet hands hard and then stops them suddenly. Why does the water fly off?
column14: The water's inertia keeps it moving after his hands stop
column15: His hands push the water away with a reaction force
column17: The water has no mass
column28: The water is moving with his hands. When his hands stop, nothing stops the water, so its inertia keeps it moving and it flies off (Newton's 1st law). Water has mass, and gravity pulls down, not sideways.
column29: When his hands stop, what does the moving water want to keep doing?

column9: Which object has the **most** inertia?
column14: A loaded semi truck
column17: A tennis ball
column28: More mass = more inertia. The loaded semi truck has by far the most mass, so it is the hardest to start moving and the hardest to stop.
column29: Inertia depends on how much mass an object has.

column9: In Newton's 2nd law, F = m × a, what does the **m** stand for?
column14: Mass, in kilograms
column17: Momentum, in kg·m/s
column28: In F = m × a, F is the net force (N), m is the mass (kg), and a is the acceleration (m/s^{2}).
column29: Which of the choices is measured in kg?

column9: To find an object's **acceleration** from the net force on it and its mass, which formula do you use?
column14: a = F ÷ m
column17: a = F − m
column28: Rearrange F = m × a by dividing both sides by the mass: a = F ÷ m. The force goes on top.
column29: Start from F = m × a and get a by itself.

column9: A 10 kg wagon accelerates at 3 m/s^{2}. What net force acts on it? Answer in N.
column28: Formula: F = m × a. Set up: F = 10 kg × 3 m/s^{2}. Answer: 30 N.
column29: Force = mass × acceleration.

column9: A 2 kg ball accelerates at 4.5 m/s^{2}. What net force acts on it? Answer in N.
column28: Formula: F = m × a. Set up: F = 2 kg × 4.5 m/s^{2}. Answer: 9 N.
column29: Force = mass × acceleration.

column9: A net force of 20 N pushes a 4 kg cart. What is the cart's acceleration? Answer in m/s^{2}.
column28: Formula: a = F ÷ m. Set up: a = 20 N ÷ 4 kg. Answer: 5 m/s^{2}.
column29: Acceleration = force ÷ mass.

column9: A net force of 60 N gives a box an acceleration of 2 m/s^{2}. What is the box's mass? Answer in kg.
column28: Formula: m = F ÷ a. Set up: m = 60 N ÷ 2 m/s^{2}. Answer: 30 kg. Multiplying (120) is the common mistake.
column29: Mass = force ÷ acceleration.

column9: A net force of 45 N acts on a 15 kg sled. What is the sled's acceleration? Answer in m/s^{2}.
column28: Formula: a = F ÷ m. Set up: a = 45 N ÷ 15 kg. Answer: 3 m/s^{2}.
column29: Put the force on top and the mass on the bottom.

column9: A soccer ball sits still on the field. According to Newton's 1st law, what will it take to get the ball moving?
column14: An unbalanced force, like a kick
column15: Nothing; it will start rolling on its own
column16: Waiting for gravity to push it sideways
column17: A pair of balanced forces
column28: An object at rest stays at rest unless an unbalanced force acts on it. A kick gives the ball a net force, so it starts moving. Balanced forces cause no change in motion.
column29: What does the 1st law say an object at rest will keep doing?

column9: When a car turns a sharp corner, the passengers slide toward the outside of the curve. Why?
column14: Their inertia keeps their bodies moving in a straight line while the car turns
column17: The seatbelts pull them toward the doors
column28: Because of inertia, a passenger's body keeps moving in a straight line. The car turns under them, so they seem to slide toward the outside until the door or seatbelt pushes them along the curve.
column29: If nothing pushed on your body, which way would it keep going?

column9: A rider is on a horse that stops suddenly at a fence. Which way does the rider tend to move, and why?
column14: Forward, because of inertia
column15: Backward, because the horse pushes back
column17: Nowhere; the rider stops at the same instant as the horse
column28: The rider was moving forward with the horse. When the horse stops, the rider's inertia keeps the rider moving forward until something (the saddle, the reins, or the ground) stops them.
column29: Before the horse stops, which way is the rider moving?

column9: Mr. Erickson hangs a dusty rug on a line and smacks it with a broom. The dust falls out. Which idea best explains why?
column14: Inertia: the rug jerks away, but the dust tends to stay where it was
column15: The broom pushes each piece of dust out on purpose
column16: Friction pulls the dust toward the broom
column17: The dust has no mass, so it floats away
column28: The rug jerks suddenly when it is hit, but the dust's inertia keeps it at rest, so the rug moves out from under the dust and the dust falls away. That is Newton's 1st law.
column29: Which part moves suddenly, and which part tends to stay where it was?

column9: Which situation shows **balanced** forces on an object?
column14: A lamp hanging still from the ceiling
column15: A car speeding up on an on-ramp
column16: A dropped ball falling faster and faster
column17: A bike slowing down as it coasts
column28: Balanced forces cause no change in motion, so the hanging lamp stays at rest. The other three are speeding up or slowing down, which takes an unbalanced force.
column29: Balanced forces mean the motion does not change. Which object's motion is not changing?

column9: What do **unbalanced** forces always cause?
column14: A change in motion: speeding up, slowing down, or turning
column17: An object to lose mass
column28: An unbalanced force (a net force) changes an object's motion. It can speed the object up, slow it down, or change its direction. It does not change the object's mass.
column29: Unbalanced forces leave a net force. What does a net force do?

column9: The same net force pushes a 5 kg cart and a 10 kg cart. Which cart has the greater acceleration?
column14: The 5 kg cart
column17: Neither cart accelerates
column28: a = F ÷ m. With the same force, the smaller mass gets the bigger acceleration: the 5 kg cart accelerates twice as much as the 10 kg cart.
column29: Same push: does more mass make a cart speed up more or less?

column9: Which change will make a cart's acceleration **smaller** if the push stays the same?
column14: Adding more mass to the cart
column16: Taking some mass out of the cart
column17: Oiling the wheels so there is less friction
column28: With the same force, more mass means less acceleration. Pushing harder, removing mass, or cutting friction (which raises the net force) all make the acceleration bigger.
column29: Think about pushing an empty cart and a full cart with the same push.

column9: If the mass stays the same, force and acceleration have a ___ relationship: double the net force and you double the acceleration.
column28: Direct: when the force goes up, the acceleration goes up by the same factor (a = F ÷ m). Mass and acceleration are the ones that go opposite ways.
column29: When one goes up and the other goes up too, what kind of relationship is that?

column9: An object moving at a constant speed in a straight line must have an unbalanced force acting on it to keep it moving.
column28: False. An object in motion stays in motion at a constant speed in a straight line when the forces on it are balanced. An unbalanced force would change its motion.
column29: Does a hockey puck on smooth ice need a push to keep sliding?

column9: Far out in space, a heavy toolbox weighs almost nothing. Is it still hard to push it to get it moving?
column14: Yes, because it still has its mass, and mass gives it inertia
column15: No, because things in space have no inertia
column16: No, because it has almost no weight
column17: Yes, because gravity in space is extra strong
column28: Inertia depends on mass, not weight. The toolbox has the same mass in space, so it still resists starting (and stopping), even though it weighs almost nothing.
column29: Does inertia depend on mass or on weight?

column9: What is the net force on a 3 kg box that accelerates at 4 m/s^{2}?
column28: Formula: F = m × a. Set up: F = 3 kg × 4 m/s^{2}. Answer: 12 N. 0.75 and 1.33 come from dividing, and 7 comes from adding.
column29: Force = mass × acceleration.

column9: A ball rolls across the gym floor and slowly comes to a stop. According to Newton's 1st law, why does it stop?
column14: An unbalanced force, friction, acts on it
column15: Moving objects naturally run out of motion
column17: Gravity pulls it backward
column28: An object in motion stays in motion unless an unbalanced force acts on it. Friction from the floor (and air resistance) points opposite the motion and slows the ball. Inertia is not used up, and gravity points down, not backward.
column29: What force works against a rolling ball?

column9: A hockey puck slides across the ice at a constant velocity (ignore friction). What is the net force on the puck?
column14: 0 N
column15: The same as the puck's weight
column16: A small forward force that keeps it moving
column17: It depends on how fast the puck is going
column28: Constant velocity means the motion is not changing, so the forces are balanced and the net force is 0 N. No forward force is needed to keep it sliding.
column29: If the motion is not changing, are the forces balanced or unbalanced?

column9: Which needs a bigger net force to accelerate at 2 m/s^{2}: a 10 kg box or a 20 kg box?
column14: The 20 kg box
column17: Neither box needs a force
column28: F = m × a. For the same acceleration, more mass needs more force: 20 kg × 2 m/s^{2} = 40 N, but 10 kg × 2 m/s^{2} = 20 N.
column29: Use F = m × a for each box.

column9: Match each of Newton's laws to what it says.
column14: Newton's 1st law :: An object keeps doing what it is doing unless an unbalanced force acts on it
column15: Newton's 2nd law :: Acceleration depends on the net force and the mass (F = m × a)
column16: Newton's 3rd law :: Every action force has an equal and opposite reaction force
column28: 1st law = inertia (things keep doing what they are doing). 2nd law = F = m × a. 3rd law = action-reaction pairs.
column29: Inertia = 1st, F = ma = 2nd, pairs of forces = 3rd.

column9: Maya wants the net force on a 7 kg cart that accelerates at 2 m/s^{2}. Which setup is correct?
column28: Formula: F = m × a. Set up: F = 7 kg × 2 m/s^{2}. Answer: 14 N.
column29: Newton's 2nd law: force = mass × acceleration.

column9: Why does loose cargo slide toward the back of a pickup truck bed when the truck speeds up quickly?
column14: The cargo's inertia keeps it at rest while the truck moves forward under it
column15: The truck pushes the cargo backward
column16: Gravity pulls the cargo toward the back
column17: The cargo gets lighter when the truck speeds up
column28: When the truck speeds up, the cargo's inertia tends to keep it where it was (at rest), so the truck bed slides forward under it. That is why loads need a tailgate or straps.
column29: Before the truck speeds up, the cargo is at rest. What does it want to keep doing?

column9: In F = m × a, force is measured in ___.
column28: Force is measured in newtons (N). 1 N = 1 kg·m/s^{2}, a mass times an acceleration.
column29: The unit is named after the scientist who wrote the laws of motion.

column9: A train moves at a steady 30 m/s along a straight track. Which statement is true?
column14: The forces on the train are balanced
column15: There is a net force forward on the train
column16: There is a net force backward on the train
column17: There are no forces on the train at all
column28: A steady speed in a straight line means the motion is not changing, so the forces are balanced (net force 0 N). The engine's push balances friction and air resistance; the forces don't disappear.
column29: Is the train's motion changing?

column9: To find an object's **mass** from the net force on it and its acceleration, which formula do you use?
column14: m = F ÷ a
column17: m = F − a
column28: Rearrange F = m × a by dividing both sides by the acceleration: m = F ÷ a.
column29: Start from F = m × a and get m by itself.

column9: Wyatt and his bike have a total mass of 68 kg and accelerate at 2.5 m/s^{2}. What net force acts on them? Answer in N.
column28: Formula: F = m × a. Set up: F = 68 kg × 2.5 m/s^{2}. Answer: 170 N.
column29: Multiply the mass by the acceleration.

column9: A 380 kg snowmobile with its rider is pushed by a net force of 1,140 N. What is its acceleration? Answer in m/s^{2}.
column28: Formula: a = F ÷ m. Set up: a = 1,140 N ÷ 380 kg. Answer: 3 m/s^{2}.
column29: Acceleration = force ÷ mass.

column9: A net force of 1,800 N gives a fishing boat an acceleration of 4.5 m/s^{2}. What is the boat's mass? Answer in kg.
column28: Formula: m = F ÷ a. Set up: m = 1,800 N ÷ 4.5 m/s^{2}. Answer: 400 kg.
column29: Mass = force ÷ acceleration.

column9: A tennis racket gives a 0.058 kg tennis ball an acceleration of 1,500 m/s^{2}. What net force does the racket put on the ball? Answer in N.
column28: Formula: F = m × a. Set up: F = 0.058 kg × 1,500 m/s^{2}. Answer: 87 N. A tiny mass with a huge acceleration still takes a big force.
column29: Force = mass × acceleration, even for a small mass.

column9: A cart accelerates at 3.0 m/s^{2}. Half of its load is taken out, so its mass is cut in half, and the net force stays the same. What is the new acceleration?
column28: Mass and acceleration have an inverse relationship: cut the mass in half and the acceleration doubles. 3.0 m/s^{2} × 2 = 6.0 m/s^{2}.
column29: With the same force, does a lighter cart speed up more or less?

column9: Group A pushes a 5 kg cart with different forces and records: 10 N → 2 m/s^{2}, 20 N → 4 m/s^{2}, 30 N → 6 m/s^{2}. What relationship does the data show between force and acceleration?
column14: Direct: when the force doubles, the acceleration doubles
column15: Inverse: when the force doubles, the acceleration is cut in half
column17: The acceleration stays the same no matter the force
column28: Each time the force goes up by 10 N, the acceleration goes up by 2 m/s^{2}, and doubling the force (10 N → 20 N) doubles the acceleration (2 → 4). That is a direct relationship, and every row fits F = m × a with m = 5 kg.
column29: Compare the 10 N row with the 20 N row. What happened to the acceleration?

column9: A lab cart's data table shows: 4 N → 0.5 m/s^{2}, 8 N → 1.0 m/s^{2}, 12 N → 1.5 m/s^{2}. What is the cart's mass? Answer in kg.
column28: Use any row with m = F ÷ a. Set up: m = 4 N ÷ 0.5 m/s^{2}. Answer: 8 kg. (8 ÷ 1.0 and 12 ÷ 1.5 give the same mass.)
column29: Pick one row and use mass = force ÷ acceleration.

column9: Which statements about inertia are true? Select all that apply.
column14: Inertia depends on mass
column16: A moving object keeps moving unless an unbalanced force acts on it
column17: Lighter objects have more inertia than heavier objects
column18: Inertia only acts on objects that are moving
column28: Inertia is a property that depends on mass (more mass = more inertia), not a force. It resists any change in motion, so objects at rest and objects in motion both have it. Heavier objects have more inertia, not less.
column29: Think about a bowling ball sitting still and a bowling ball rolling. Do both resist changes?

column9: Which of these needs the **greatest** net force?
column14: A 2 kg cart accelerating at 9 m/s^{2}
column15: A 3 kg cart accelerating at 5 m/s^{2}
column16: A 6 kg cart accelerating at 2 m/s^{2}
column17: A 12 kg cart accelerating at 1 m/s^{2}
column28: F = m × a for each: 2 × 9 = 18 N, 3 × 5 = 15 N, 6 × 2 = 12 N, and 12 × 1 = 12 N. The 2 kg cart needs the most force, even though it has the least mass.
column29: Find F = m × a for each cart before you decide.

column9: A 1,000 kg car and a 4,000 kg truck are each pushed by the same net force. How do their accelerations compare?
column14: The car's acceleration is 4 times the truck's
column15: The truck's acceleration is 4 times the car's
column17: The car's acceleration is one-fourth of the truck's
column28: With the same force, acceleration is inverse to mass. The truck has 4 times the mass, so it gets one-fourth the acceleration; the car's acceleration is 4 times the truck's.
column29: Same force: which vehicle speeds up more, the lighter one or the heavier one?

column9: A 0.6 kg basketball at rest is pushed by a player's hands for 0.15 s and leaves at 9 m/s. What net force did the hands apply? Answer in N.
column29: Find the acceleration first (change in velocity ÷ time), then use F = m × a.

column9: Jacob pushes a 20 kg box to the right with 110 N. Friction pushes on the box 30 N to the left. What is the box's acceleration? Answer in m/s^{2}.
column28: Net force: 110 N − 30 N = 80 N to the right. Formula: a = F ÷ m. Set up: a = 80 N ÷ 20 kg. Answer: 4 m/s^{2} to the right. Using 110 N instead of the net force is the common mistake.
column29: Find the net force first (opposite directions subtract), then use a = F ÷ m.

column9: A 1,100 kg car speeds up from 0 m/s to 22 m/s in 8.0 s on Hwy 29. What net force acts on it? Answer in N.
column29: Step 1: a = Δv ÷ t. Step 2: F = m × a.

column9: A lab cart speeds up from 2 m/s to 8 m/s in 3 s. The net force on it is 24 N. What is the cart's mass? Answer in kg.
column28: Step 1: a = Δv ÷ t = (8 m/s − 2 m/s) ÷ 3 s = 2 m/s^{2}. Step 2: m = F ÷ a = 24 N ÷ 2 m/s^{2} = 12 kg. Using 8 m/s instead of the change in velocity is the common mistake.
column29: The change in velocity is final minus starting. Find a, then use mass = force ÷ acceleration.

column9: A wagon accelerates at 2.4 m/s^{2}. Then the net force on it is cut in half AND its mass is doubled. What is the new acceleration? Answer in m/s^{2}.
column28: Half the force cuts the acceleration in half (2.4 → 1.2 m/s^{2}). Double the mass cuts it in half again (1.2 → 0.6 m/s^{2}). Answer: 0.6 m/s^{2}, one-fourth of the start.
column29: Do one change at a time. What does each change do to the acceleration?

column9: Saffron wants a 30 kg sled to accelerate at 0.8 m/s^{2}. Friction on the sled is 40 N, pointing backward. How hard must she pull forward? Answer in N.
column28: Step 1: net force needed: F = m × a = 30 kg × 0.8 m/s^{2} = 24 N. Step 2: her pull must beat friction AND supply that net force: 24 N + 40 N = 64 N.
column29: F = m × a gives the net force. Her pull minus friction has to equal that net force.

column9: Storm says, "Newton's 1st law means moving objects naturally slow down and stop." Which response is best?
column14: She is wrong; moving objects slow down only when an unbalanced force, like friction, acts on them
column15: She is right; all moving objects run out of motion
column16: She is right; an object's inertia slowly wears off
column17: She is wrong; moving objects always speed up
column28: An object in motion stays in motion at a constant speed in a straight line unless an unbalanced force acts on it. On Earth, friction and air resistance are usually that force, which is why things seem to stop on their own. Inertia does not wear off.
column29: Think of a space probe with nothing around it. Would it slow down?

column9: On the International Space Station, an astronaut pushes a 30 kg bag of supplies with a net force of 45 N. The bag is weightless, but it still has mass. What is its acceleration? Answer in m/s^{2}.
column28: Mass does not change in space, so F = m × a still works. Formula: a = F ÷ m. Set up: a = 45 N ÷ 30 kg. Answer: 1.5 m/s^{2}.
column29: Weightless does not mean massless. Use a = F ÷ m.

column9: Two forces act on a 4 kg box: 50 N to the right and 30 N to the left. What is the box's acceleration?
column14: 5 m/s^{2} to the right
column17: 5 m/s^{2} to the left
column28: Net force: 50 N − 30 N = 20 N to the right. a = F ÷ m = 20 N ÷ 4 kg = 5 m/s^{2} to the right. 20 m/s^{2} comes from adding the forces, and 12.5 m/s^{2} uses only the 50 N force.
column29: Find the net force first, then divide by the mass.

column9: Jae pushes a 2 kg cart and Addy pushes a 6 kg cart, each with a 12 N net force, for 2 s. Both carts start at rest. Which statement is true?
column14: The 2 kg cart ends up going 3 times as fast (12 m/s vs. 4 m/s)
column15: Both carts end up at the same speed
column16: The 6 kg cart ends up going 3 times as fast
column17: Neither cart moves, because the two forces are equal
column28: 2 kg cart: a = 12 N ÷ 2 kg = 6 m/s^{2}, so after 2 s it is going 6 × 2 = 12 m/s. 6 kg cart: a = 12 N ÷ 6 kg = 2 m/s^{2}, so it reaches 2 × 2 = 4 m/s. Same force, one-third the mass, three times the speed.
column29: Find each cart's acceleration with a = F ÷ m, then speed = acceleration × time.
